1:
The address is weighed by all. Gill hears the writer’s age in it, and his fatherhood, since he was the instrument of their conversion. Henry divides the phrase into three: children as begotten by his gospel, little children as beneath him in age and experience, my little children as dear to him in the bonds of the gospel — adding that the gospel most prevailed where such ministerial love abounded.

Why the purpose clause is there is Calvin’s question, and he makes it the hinge of the chapter. It is not only the sum of the preceding doctrine but the meaning of almost the whole gospel that we are to depart from sin; and he anticipates the objection that mercy licenses it. The doctrine of grace has always been calumniated by the ungodly, who boast, when the expiation of sins is set forth, that a license is given to sin. Yet though heaven should fall, this part of the truth ought never to be omitted; the barkings of the ungodly are to be disregarded, since the apostles were assailed by the same. Henry suggests the clause may be rendered, these things write I unto you, not that you sin — looking back to the pardon just promised, and so precluding abuse of it, or forward to the Advocate.

The comfort to the fallen is warm. Clarke tells the backslider his case is deeply deplorable but not desperate, and glosses the command as a call to happiness: do not run into ruin, live not so as to promote your own misery, for holiness and happiness are inseparable. Wesley describes the Advocate by what he is not: not a mean person, not a guilty one needing pardon, not a mere petitioner relying on liberality, but one who has fully merited whatever he asks. Robertson distributes the title — the Holy Spirit is God’s Advocate on earth, Christ man’s Advocate with the Father — and observes that the writer has no patience with professional perfectionists, and still less with loose-livers.

On the word for propitiation Barnes does the work. It occurs nowhere else in the New Testament but once more in this letter, and its proper sense is reconciling, appeasing, turning away anger, as often in the older poets. He then guards the idea against being taken too literally and against being explained away: God’s law has been violated and he has reason to be offended; he cannot consistently treat us as if we had not done it; it is proper he should show his displeasure, by punishing us or by something answering the same purpose; and the means of propitiation come in and accomplish that end. Clarke fills in the Greek Old Testament uses, where the word stands for the sin-offering and the atonement; Robertson puts it in a line: he himself in his own person is both priest and sacrifice.

The last clause opens the sharpest disagreement here. Gill restricts it hardest: our sins means the sins of us who now believe and are Jews. Clarke goes to the opposite pole: the apostle does not say Christ died for any select part of the earth’s inhabitants, nor for some out of every nation, but for all mankind, and the attempt to limit this is a violent outrage against God and his word. Wesley says it in a sentence: as wide as sin extends, the propitiation extends also. Calvin stands between, and is the most interesting. He dismisses without refutation the notion that all the reprobate are saved, reports the scholastic formula that Christ suffered sufficiently for the whole world but efficiently only for the elect — then, having allowed it true, denies that it suits this passage, since the design here was to make the benefit common to the whole Church, so that by the whole world are meant those who should believe as well as those then scattered abroad.
3:
Two name the opponents, and the naming shapes the passage. Robertson says the Gnostics boasted of their superior knowledge of Christ, and that the writer challenges the boast by appealing to experimental knowledge shown in keeping commandments; at the next verse he is blunter, calling the claim cheap claptrap of men who would bob up in meetings with such explosions, which the sharp addition ‘and keepeth not’ punctures — there is a whip-cracker effect in the words. Clarke says it from the moral side: they pretended to much knowledge, but it left them in possession of all their bad passions and unholy habits, so they gave no proof of having known either God or his Son; and he extends the blow to all who boast in the righteousness of Christ as a covering for their personal unholiness.

Calvin makes the same complaint against a different party. Nothing is more common than to draw the doctrine of religion into frigid speculations, and so theology has been adulterated by the schoolmen, from whose whole science not the least spark of true religion shines forth; curious men learn just so much of God’s word as enables them to prattle for display, and no evil has been more common in all ages than vainly to profess God’s name. Then he reaches for an unexpected witness: a pagan philosopher, groping in darkness, denied that the beautiful he imagined could be known without filling a man with admiration of it — how then is it possible to know God and be moved by no feeling?

Henry sets the two ages of a Christian against each other. Young Christians are apt to magnify their new light and applaud their own knowledge, especially if it came suddenly; old ones suspect the fullness of theirs, and lament that they know God and the contents of his gospel no more. The evidence of soundness is the same in both, that the knowledge constrains them to keep God’s commandments. Gill puts the distinction in the object: this is not knowing God with fear and trembling as the devils know him, nor in theory as formal professors and hypocrites do, but with a knowledge joined to hearty love and cheerful obedience.

What it means for love to be perfected is the one real division. Barnes guards it hard. The passage makes no affirmation about sinless perfection; it affirms only that if true love exists in the heart it will be carried out in the life, that love and obedience are parts of one thing, and that neither can fully develop without the other. Wesley, from whom one might expect the opposite, is weaker still, glossing perfected simply as perfectly known.

Calvin turns the verse into a definition and faces the objection. To love God in sincerity of heart is what keeping his commandments means, for the law, being spiritual, does not command external works only but enjoins loving God with the whole heart; and if any objects that no man was ever found who loved God thus perfectly, it is enough that every one aspire to that perfection according to the measure of grace given him.

On abiding, two of them build the same ladder. Wesley makes knowing him, being in him, and abiding in him nearly synonymous but graded — knowledge, communion, constancy; Clarke divides the same ground, being in Christ meaning conversion and remission of sins, abiding in him continuance in that state and growth in grace. Calvin adds that the apostle does not merely exhort us to imitate Christ but argues from the union we have with him that we ought to be like him. Wesley closes with an observation about the writer’s manner: the words ‘as he’ occur constantly in this epistle, because believers, having their hearts full of him, easily supply his name.
7:
The paradox is stated plainly and explained three ways. Robertson calls it paradox but truth: old in teaching, as old as Cain and Abel, but new in practice, as love is as old as man and fresh in every experience. Clarke admits the appearance of contradiction and resolves it by dispensations: the difference lies not in the essence of the precept but in the degrees of light and grace belonging to the Mosaic and the Christian orders. God always commanded men to love one another, but Christ renewed it with much latitude of meaning, and with the addition that we should love the brethren so as to lay down our lives for each other. Calvin explains why the oldness needed stressing. Novelty is disliked or suspected, we do not easily undertake an unwonted yoke, and once we have embraced a doctrine we dislike having anything in it changed; so he reminds them that he taught nothing about love but what they had heard from the beginning.

Henry runs the precept back through the ages. It must be as old as human nature, though it admitted different enactments: in innocence men would have loved one another as of one blood and bearing God’s image; after the fall, as related to their Maker and partners in the same hope; and when the Hebrews were incorporated, as the privileged people of whose race the Messiah must spring. Gill adds a Jewish expectation that pays the paradox back: they looked for a new law from the Messiah, and a new one he has given, the commandment of love.

Calvin takes the newness as perpetual freshness. The elements children learn give place to something higher, but this doctrine never grows old; and since men are more curious than they ought to be, many always seek something new, so that there arises a weariness of simple doctrine which produces innumerable prodigies of errors. What greater revelation can be expected, when Christ is the end and completion of all things? Let him who would reach the goal of wisdom make proficiency in love.

Three notice how carefully the dawn is described. Clarke presses the tenses: he does not say the darkness was all gone by, but that it is passing away; nor that the fullness of the light had appeared, but that it is now shining and will shine more to the perfect day, as the darkness passes in proportion as the light increases. Robertson agrees that night does pass by even if slowly, but leaves open what is meant: the second coming, or the slow victory of truth over error.

Who the brother is divides them: Barnes restricts it to those professing the same religion, to what is properly brotherly love among Christians; Clarke widens it to his neighbour, his fellow creature, whether Jew or Gentile.

The stumbling-block divides them again, and Robertson names the ambiguity: the word usually means a trap in the way of others, but it may mean one in a man’s own way, and both senses may be in play across the two verses. Barnes takes it of the man himself: where love is, there is nothing on his side to lead him into sin, for envy and malice can have no place in one who loves his brother. Clarke wants both at once: he neither gives offence nor receives it, since love keeps him from giving any and leads him to put the best construction on everything; and walking in the light he sees the stumbling-blocks and avoids them, for many fall into sin because they do not see the snares. Wesley turns it inward: he who hates his brother stumbles against himself and against all things within and without, while he who loves has a free, disencumbered journey. Robertson closes with an image nobody else could have supplied: in the Mammoth Cave the fish have eye-sockets, but no eyes.
12:
The repetition is the first problem, and it splits them cleanly. Barnes reports that some found the tautology so awkward that one commentator supposed error had crept into the text and part of these verses should be dropped; he refuses, since there is no authority for omitting any of it, and the passage is very much in the apostle’s general style. Calvin takes the other side: these repetitions he deems superfluous, and thinks it probable that unskilful readers, falsely supposing the writer spoke twice of little children, rashly introduced the other two clauses. Robertson settles it by grammar and temper: the verbs are epistolary aorists referring to this letter, not an earlier one, and though one scholar suggests the writer was interrupted and resumed, that is needless ingenuity, for it is quite in his style to repeat himself with slight variations.

How many classes are addressed is the second. Clarke counts four, and his reason is lexical: the word for little children in the second address differs from the one in the first, so that if the apostle does not use them indifferently, four states are described and not three. Everyone else counts three. Calvin insists the first word means men of all ages and that interpreters have wrongly applied it to children, since when the writer means children by age he uses the other word; Robertson says it probably includes all; Wesley treats it as the address to the whole body, after which the three ranks are taken in order and each enlarged upon through the rest of the chapter.

Calvin makes the threefold address pastoral strategy. A general address sometimes produces less effect, for such is our perversity that few think what is addressed to all belongs to them: the old excuse themselves as past the age of learning, children refuse to learn as not yet old enough, and men of middle age do not attend, being occupied with other pursuits. So the gospel is accommodated to each. He then recalls that the Spartan chorus had three orders, the first singing what ye are we shall be, the last what ye are we have been, and the middle we are what one of you has been and the other will be.

What the fathers are said to know is disputed by two of them in the same terms. Clarke thinks they were converts from the very commencement of Christianity, some of whom had probably seen Christ in the flesh, though he allows that him who is from the beginning may equally mean Christ in the eternity of his nature. Gill supplies a different background, that the Jews called their men of wisdom fathers, and that a whole treatise of the Mishna bears the name. Robertson notes the perfect tense in the young men’s clause, a permanent victory after conflict, and that the masculine article shows the prince of darkness to be the one defeated.

Two of them use the passage to guard something larger. Calvin warns that holiness of life ought to be urged and men sharply goaded to repentance, but that we must take heed lest the doctrine of faith be smothered, and such moderation be kept that faith retains its primacy; the free remission of sins is set here so that the preceding exhortation should not obscure it. Augustine of Hippo, opening a homily on the letter, says that of all read from the Scriptures for our instruction, most of all must those things be commended to memory which are of most force against heretics, whose designs never cease to circumvent the weaker and more negligent; and he recalls the two on the road whose eyes were holden, who knew the Lord only in the breaking of bread. Henry adds the moral: wise pastors will distribute the word of life judiciously, giving the several members of Christ’s family their suitable portions.
15:
Barnes distinguishes three senses of the word, and only the third is forbidden. There is the physical universe, which it is not improper to love, since we may suppose God loves his own works; the world of mankind, whom it is not wrong to love with a love of benevolence, including kindred and friends who are not Christians; and the community that lives by maxims having reference only to this life, on which alone the affections may not be fixed. Calvin explains why the prohibition comes first: until our minds are cleansed, the doctrine of loving God may be iterated a hundred times with no effect, for it would be like pouring water on a ball, from which not a drop can be gathered because there is no empty place to hold it.

Clarke turns the command back on the three ranks just addressed. Covetousness is the predominant vice of old age, so, ye fathers, love not the world; the profits, pleasures and honours of the world have the strongest allurements for youth, so, ye young men and babes, love not the things of the world. Wesley makes the same connection in a line: pursue your victory by overcoming the world. Gill draws the boundary on the other side: the men of the world are to be loved as fellow creatures and their good sought, but their company is not to be preferred to the saints’, nor their ways imitated.

On the three lusts they diverge, most sharply over the second. Henry takes the lust of the eyes as covetousness plainly, the eyes being delighted with riches and rich possessions; Clarke fills that out with inordinate desires after finery of every kind, gaudy dress, splendid houses and expensive equipage. Wesley reads it quite differently, as the pleasures of imagination, to which the eye is chiefly subservient — that internal sense whereby we relish whatever is grand, new or beautiful — and puts covetousness under the third head, with the desire of praise. Robertson keeps all three as subjective genitives and reaches for a modern instance, the use of moving pictures for gain by lustful exhibitions; he reports the suggestion that these three, like the temptation in the garden and the temptations of Christ, cover all possible sins, and states the standing problem: how to be in the world and yet not of it.

Calvin declines the usual reading of the first phrase, which takes flesh for the whole corrupt nature and its lust for sinful desire in general. He prefers the narrower sense, the body and all that belongs to it, so that the lust of the flesh appears when worldly men, seeking to live softly, are intent only on their own advantage. He then answers an ancient philosopher’s division of desires into the natural and necessary, the natural but unnecessary, and the neither natural nor necessary: the apostle, knowing the insubordination of the human heart, condemns the lust of the flesh outright, because it always flows out immoderately and never observes any due medium.

The last verse turns the argument into comfort. Barnes says these things pass like the shifting scenes of a stage, or a pageant which amuses the eye a moment and disappears; abiding for ever cannot mean the man will not die, but that he has built his happiness on a secure basis. Robertson finds consolation in the same transitoriness, since the conflict with the world is itself passing. Calvin meets the objection that no one actually does the will of God: what is spoken of is not the perfect keeping of the law but the obedience of faith, which, however imperfect, is yet approved by God. Gill lists what is going — kingdoms, cities, families, estates, one generation for another — and concludes that everything is in flux and nothing permanent.
18:
What the last hour means draws five answers. Gill makes it the last hour of the apostolic age, since all the apostles were now dead and John was the last of them. Henry takes it of the Jewish polity hastening to an end, with Daniel’s weeks expiring and the destruction of the city approaching. Clarke canvasses the options, including the suggestion that the phrase means a perilous time rather than a chronological last, and thinks the letter was written while Jerusalem yet stood. Barnes prefers the last dispensation, and guards it: the apostle does not say the end would soon occur, and that period might continue through many ages and still be the last. Robertson leaves it open: a period, a series, or the final climax just at hand.

Calvin alone states the objection time has raised against the verse. So many ages having passed since the writer’s death seem to prove the prophecy untrue; he replies that the apostle declares, after the common manner of Scripture, that nothing now remained but that Christ should appear, and that since he fixes no time he neither allured that age with a vain hope nor meant to cut short the Church’s long course. If the eternity of God’s kingdom be borne in mind, so long a time will appear as a moment.

On the word antichrist, Barnes does the philology and Clarke draws the conclusion. Barnes lists the senses the preposition carries in composition — over against, contrary to, reciprocity, substitution — so the word might denote one claiming to stand in Christ’s place or one simply opposed to him. Clarke names no candidate. Is it the emperor, the Gnostics, the Cerinthians, the Roman pontiffs? Any person, doctrine or system opposed to Christ and to the spread of his gospel is antichrist, and we need not look for an imaginary being in any of these exclusively — even Protestantism may have its antichrist as well as Popery. Wesley agrees that the term includes all false teachers and enemies of the truth, and notes that only long after this was the name appropriated to one grand adversary. Robertson adds that his use of it is determined by the Christian conception, not by the Jewish apocalypses.

Augustine of Hippo takes the address to children as a summons to grow. Stature of the body is not at one’s own will, and a man does not grow in the flesh when he wills, any more than he is born when he wills; but where the being born rests with the will, the growth rests with the will too. Let him who knows he is born hear that he is an infant, and cling to the breasts of his mother the Church, which are the two Testaments, that being nourished he may attain to solid meat. Our milk, he says, is Christ in his humility; our meat, the selfsame Christ equal with the Father.

The verse about those who went out is used two ways. Barnes makes it a proof of perseverance: the affirmation is unqualified that if they had been true Christians they would have remained, and may be taken as a universal truth. Calvin agrees, and sorts professors into three kinds: those who feign piety while a bad conscience reproves them, those whose hypocrisy dazzles their own eyes so that they seem to themselves to worship God aright, and those who have the living root of faith and the testimony of their adoption fixed in their hearts. Clarke dissents on the last clause: the false teachers probably drew many sincere souls away with them, and this is why the apostle says they were not all of us — some were, others were not. Cyril of Jerusalem supplies the oldest application, making the verse describe the man who tried to buy the Spirit with money and became, in his account, the inventor of all heresy.
20:
Two of them notice the same thing independently. Wesley suggests the anointing is perhaps so termed in opposition to the name of antichrist just used; Robertson makes the same guess, and adds that Christians are themselves anointed ones, while those antichrists posed as the equals of Christ or even his superiors. Clarke insists the Greek means not an unction but an ointment, the very thing by which anointing is effected, and traces it to the holy oil of the law compounded of myrrh, cinnamon, calamus, cassia and olive oil. Barnes takes it as an allusion to the anointing of kings and priests, the oil being emblematic of the graces qualifying them for office, and notes that Christians are described as kings and priests and a royal priesthood. Gill adds a rabbinic note, that the Jews held the anointing oil of the law to last until the days of the Messiah, and calls these believers the wise virgins whose lamps never go out.

Who the Holy One is goes unsettled. Barnes takes it of the Holy Spirit; Clarke agrees that not only the gifts of the Spirit but the Spirit himself is meant; Robertson divides the two, saying they receive the anointing of the Spirit from the Anointed One, who is the Holy One; Henry leaves it open, and observes that the Spirit is compared to oil as well as to fire and water.

The clause about knowing all things produces three solutions. Robertson reports that the best manuscripts read not all things but all persons, so that the sense is, ye all know it — the anointing being open to every Christian and not to a select few. Clarke proposes something stranger: the word we translate all things is probably accusative singular with the word for man understood, so the verse should read, ye know or discern every man — a reading he thinks confirmed by the reference to those deceiving them a few verses later. Barnes keeps the received text but fences it in: the meaning cannot be that they knew all things pertaining to history, science and the arts, but all that is essential in religion. Clarke adds that they have no need of the knowledge of which the Gnostics boast.

Why the apostle explains himself at all is Calvin’s subject, and he turns it into a lesson for teachers. The writer excuses himself for having warned them so earnestly, lest they think themselves indirectly reproved as ignorant of what they ought to have known. Experience teaches how fastidious the ears of men are; such fastidiousness ought to be far from the godly, yet a faithful teacher must omit nothing by which he may secure a hearing from all, since we receive what is said with less attention when we think the speaker disparages the knowledge already given us. But the praise also stimulates, for those endowed with the gift of knowledge have less excuse if they do not surpass others; the aim is to rouse up the sparks of the Spirit until a full brightness shines out in them.

On the last clause Barnes writes the best paragraph here. Error often appears plausible: it seems adapted to relieve the mind of difficulties, to promote religion, to make those who embrace it happy, so that for a time they apparently enjoy religion. But however plausible, no error can have its foundation in truth, and must be worthless; the grand question is what the truth is, and when that is settled the rest can be settled too. Calvin guards the sentence against being read as a schoolroom maxim: this is not the dialectic proposition that falsehood differs from truth, but something practical — whatever deception Satan might contrive, they would readily distinguish light from darkness, because they had the Spirit as their guide. Robertson leaves one question open, whether the conjunction is causal or declarative; either makes sense.
22:
Who is described they answer from history. Barnes supposes a class who admitted that Jesus lived but denied he was the Messiah. Robertson names the same school, the Cerinthian Gnostics, who denied the identity of the man Jesus with the Christ, whom they held to be an aeon, and remarks that the modern Jesus-or-Christ controversy descends from it. He also stops over the redundant negative in the Greek after the verb to deny, noting that old English kept the same construction. Clarke fills in what the parties held: Jews and Gnostics alike denied the miraculous conception, and with both he was accounted no more than a common man, though the Gnostics allowed that a divine being dwelt in him.

Calvin will not leave it in the first century. He agrees with the ancients about the two named heretics, but says the denial extends much wider, since it is not enough to confess in words unless Christ is acknowledged to be such as the Father offers him in the gospel. Then he calls the roll. One adorned him with the name of God and robbed him of his eternal divinity; another dreamt he was a mere phantom; a third imagined he differed nothing from the Father; a fourth, allowing him true man and God, transferred to us almost all the honour belonging to him — for it is to reduce Christ to nothing when his grace and power are set aside. He ends nearer home: those who set up free will against the grace of the Spirit, ascribe part of their righteousness to works, and feign innumerable advocates, have a sort of fictitious Christ.

Calvin softens the sentence before pressing it: the apostle does not assert that these alone were liars, but that they surpassed all others — as though unless this be deemed a lie, nothing could be so reckoned, in the way we say that if perfidy towards God and men is not a crime, nothing can be called one. Wesley tightens it instead: that Jesus is the Christ, that he is the Son of God, that he came in the flesh, is one undivided truth, and he that denies any part of it in effect denies the whole. Gill lands between them: such a man is not the only liar in the world, but the greatest of liars, and this is a consummate lie, opposed to a glaring truth.

The second half of the last verse is doubtful in the English text, and two of them argue it back in. Barnes observes that the words are printed in italics as supplied by the translators, but reports that they stand in many manuscripts, in the ancient versions, and in the modern critical editions; the clause is much in the writer’s style and should be restored as genuine. Clarke assembles a fuller case, tracing the omission through the early printed English Bibles down to one printed at Rouen where the clause stands in a different letter between brackets, and listing the manuscripts, versions and ancient writers that carry it.

What the verse asserts is stated at three levels. Robertson keeps it short: our only approach to the Father is by the Son, who reveals him. Calvin calls it a remarkable sentence which ought to be reckoned among the first axioms of religion: having confessed one true God, we must add that he is no other than the one made known in Christ, for the naked majesty of God would by its brightness dazzle our eyes. Those who philosophize on divine things without him do nothing but rave, because they hold not the Head. Cyril of Jerusalem puts it as a parable of offence: it is grievous to a king that his soldier should be dishonoured, and his anger grows when a nobler officer is; but if any do despite to his only-begotten son, who shall appease the father’s indignation?
24:
Calvin will not let the appeal to the beginning stand as an argument from antiquity. Age alone does not prove a doctrine true; if we were unwilling to depart from whatever doctrine we had once embraced, that would not be perseverance but perverse obstinacy. Discrimination must come first, so that a reason for our faith is made evident from God’s word, and then let inflexible perseverance follow. He turns it against his opponents: they boast of a beginning because they imbibed their superstitions from childhood, and under that pretence reject the plain truth. Gill identifies what is to abide as the doctrine concerning the Father and the Son, the foundation of the doctrine of the Trinity; Robertson puts the charge in a phrase, not to be carried away by the new-fangled Gnostic teaching.

On the promise Barnes writes his best passage in the chapter, a list of what heaven is not promised to. No one can show that any promise of heaven is made to the mere possessor of beauty, or wealth, or talent; to the accomplished or the gay; to those distinguished for science or skill in the arts; to rank, birth or blood; to courage or strength. Whatever expectation a man entertains on such grounds must be traced to something other than a promise; the promise is limited to those who repent, believe and lead a holy life. Calvin notes the Greek can be construed two ways, eternal life standing in apposition either to the promise or the thing promised, but says the meaning is the same; and he adds that it has ever been a cause of ruin to men that, not content with Christ, they have had a hankering to wander beyond the simple doctrine of the gospel.

Two make the seducers a pastor’s rule. Calvin says it is the duty of a good pastor not only to gather a flock but to drive away wolves, for what will it avail to proclaim the pure gospel if we connive at the impostures of Satan? Robertson says the same of the writer, who is doing his part to rescue the sheep from the wolves, as Paul did. Calvin adds a caution about his own office: in vain shall I beat your ears with my voice, or rather the air, unless the Spirit speaks within you.

The hardest sentence is that they need no man to teach them, and three refuse the obvious reading. Calvin says it would have been a strange purpose if the writer meant to represent teaching as useless, and that fanatics lay hold of the passage to exclude the outward ministry from the Church; since faith is small in some, stronger in others, and perfect in none, no one knew so much that there was no room for progress. Clarke draws the same line: it is not said that those who have received the Spirit’s teaching have no further need of the ministry of the gospel, but that they have no need of such teaching as the false teachers proposed; and no man, however holy or wise, can be beyond need of gospel ministry, for they who think so give the highest proof that they have never learned of Christ. Wesley agrees in a clause, that this does not exclude our need of being taught by those who partake of the same anointing.

Barnes again uses the abiding anointing as an assurance that true Christians will not fall away. Gill supplies a curiosity, that in the Jewish mystical scheme the second number, wisdom, is surnamed the fountain of the oil of unction. Henry closes with the duty: gospel privileges oblige to gospel duties, and those anointed by the Lord Jesus abide with him. Augustine of Hippo’s block here is not exposition but the lesson as read in church, running from this verse into the next chapter, and opening by recalling where yesterday’s reading closed.
28:
The word for confidence is glossed three ways, and they agree. Barnes says it commonly means openness or boldness in speaking, but here the calm assurance arising from evidence of piety. Clarke opens it as freedom of speech, liberty of access, boldness from a conviction that our cause is good. Robertson catches the preposition in the next phrase: shame from him, as if shrinking from Christ in guilty surprise.

Henry sets the two comings against each other. When he was here before he came privately, proceeding from a womb and introduced into a stable; but when he comes again he will come from the opened heavens, and every eye shall see him. Then those who continued with him through all their temptations will lift up their heads with unspeakable triumph, knowing that their redemption comes with him; while those who deserted him will be ashamed of their unbelief, cowardice, ingratitude and folly in forsaking so glorious a Redeemer. Barnes describes the same moment inwardly: we feel ashamed when our hopes are disappointed, when our character is shown to differ from what we professed, when our pretensions to goodness are stripped off and the heart is made bare.

Two read the shame as the minister’s own. Henry points out that the apostle includes himself, so the sense is, let not us be ashamed of you as well as, you will not be ashamed of yourselves. Clarke takes it the same way: the confounding will come when it appears that those brought to Christ have apostatised, and so are not our crown of rejoicing in the day of the Lord. Wesley abandons exposition for a cry: O how will ye, nominal Christians, be ashamed in that day!

Calvin defines confidence by its opposite, the best thing here. Faith is not a naked and frigid apprehension of Christ but a lively sense of his power; and that confidence is best shown by saying it can boldly sustain the presence of Christ. They who indulge securely in their vices turn their backs on God, and obtain peace no other way than by forgetting him — the security of the flesh, which stupefies men, so that turning from God they neither dread sin nor fear death, and meanwhile shun the tribunal of Christ. But a godly confidence delights to look on God, and the godly calmly wait for Christ and do not dread his coming.

Who is called righteous divides them. Gill takes it of Christ, righteous in his nature and works as God, in his life as man, and in his office as Mediator. Ellicott and Calvin both take it of the Father, for the same reason: the phrase about being begotten shows the Father is meant, since the new birth is nowhere ascribed to the Son. Ellicott adds that the writer regards Father and Son as so essentially one that the pronoun alone would not settle it, and Calvin that this style passes abruptly from Son to Father, so the antecedent is often not the nearest word. Robertson splits the difference: the sense is plainly of God, in spite of the adjective referring to Christ.

The two verbs for knowing are weighed. Barnes notes the Greek allows either indicative or imperative in the second, and either makes sense; Robertson distinguishes them, the first intuitive knowledge, the second experimental. Ellicott renders it rather as perceive, and adds that a divine germ sent by God has come into the life, and that as body and spirit grow in the womb so the new man is gradually formed in the soul, not perfected till the future life. Barnes turns it into a test of three negative clauses and one positive; Wesley compresses it to a line, that all his children are like himself. Clarke ends by complaining that the verse belongs to the following chapter and should never have been separated from it.
